name: Adam Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Adam. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union or party, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We milk a hundred and eighty cows, but I don't milk them myself any more. In 2019 we put in two milking robots, which are machines the cows walk into when they're ready, and they milk them and record everything. So my day starts at six with the laptop, looking at which cows didn't visit, whose milk yield dropped, who might be getting mastitis, which is an udder infection. Then I'm out fetching the stragglers, feeding, scraping, and the usual battle with the slurry pump.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did the robots change your life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I sleep later, my back's better, and I can go to my daughter's for Sunday lunch, which never happened before. But the robot rings my phone at three in the morning when a cow kicks a cup off, and I'm out in my dressing gown. The cows took to the robot in a fortnight. It took me two years to stop getting up at four to check on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, great, I already use it every day, so a bit better is welcome. I ask an assistant to sort my herd data, write the feed plan and explain the milk buyer's new contract terms in plain words. At the discussion group I'm usually the one showing people how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means small gains. If it reads my herd data better, I'd spot sick cows a day earlier, which is real money. But the milk price is still set by the dairy company, and the feed price still goes up and down, so the big picture stays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try the new herd health tools in the first month, the ones that link the robot data to the vet's records. Maybe forty or fifty a month, worth it if it saves one cow. And I'd keep paying down the robot loan, we've got three years left on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, really. It's the world I'm already living in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd spot sick cows a day earlier. What's a day worth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cow with mastitis caught on day one, that's a tube of medicine and a few days of milk thrown away. Caught on day three, you might lose her for the rest of the season, or for good. A good cow's worth fifteen hundred, so a day matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the discussion group would be slow to follow you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of them, honestly, and I don't blame them. Some of them are still paying for the last gadget that didn't work. I tell them, try it on one thing, the thing you hate most, and see.

S0.say: I already use it every day, so a bit better is welcome. At the discussion group I'm usually the one showing people how.
S0.think: It means small gains, like spotting a sick cow a day earlier, which is real money. But the dairy company still sets the milk price and the feed price still swings, so the big picture stays the same.
S0.do: Tries new herd health tools linking robot data to the vet's records in the first month, at about forty or fifty a month. Keeps paying down the milking robot loan, which has three years left.
S0.feel: Calm and pleased, because it's the world he already lives in.
S0.quote: Try it on one thing, the thing you hate most, and see.
S0.fieldNote: Adam already lives with robots, having put in milking robots in 2019, so this scenario feels like home. He thinks about value in concrete terms, like the cost of a day's delay in spotting mastitis. He is patient with slower neighbours and still carries debt from his last big investment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow suits farming, we've seen this before with tractors and milking parlours. It gives people time. I'd say the government should help with training but not try to stop it, because stopping these things never works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's mostly good. I'll have more tools and fewer surprises. The hiring bit bothers me a little for my daughter Elena, she's a data analyst, not a beginner any more, but her firm's graduate scheme just got cut in half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep updating the tools on the farm as they prove themselves. I might take on a college student over the summer, because if firms hire fewer young people, farms might as well grab some. And I'd talk to Elena about learning the farm data side, because dairy needs people who can read numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit uneasy for the young ones, not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Elena ever come into the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not to milk cows, she hated the smell as a teenager. But she could do the data and the business side for us and two or three other dairies, from home. I'd pay her, and so would they, if she was good, and she is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said stopping these things never works. Is there anything you'd want slowed down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The data side, maybe. The milk company already wants my robot data, and I'm not sure what they'd do with it. I'd want rules on that, but I'd still use the tools.

S1.say: Slow suits farming, like it did with tractors and milking parlours. The government should help with training but not try to stop it, because stopping these things never works.
S1.think: For me it's mostly good, with more tools and fewer surprises. The hiring part bothers me a little for my daughter Elena, whose firm just halved its graduate scheme.
S1.do: Keeps upgrading farm tools as they prove themselves and takes on a college student over the summer. Suggests Elena run the farm data and business side for his dairy and a few others from home.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a bit uneasy for young people but not for himself.
S1.quote: Not to milk cows, she hated the smell as a teenager.
S1.fieldNote: His centrist and adaptive sides meet here: help with training, don't try to stop change. He sees an opening for his daughter in rural data work. He still wants rules on who owns farm data, a small sign of caution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's be practical: support people who lose jobs, retrain them, and don't let the arguing stop anyone doing anything. I'd say both parties are making it worse by shouting. That's what I'd say at the discussion group and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't touch the cows. It might touch Elena's job, and my wife Sofia's hair salon, if people in town have less money. And the milk company would probably use these assistants to squeeze contract terms, which worries me more than people realise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use an assistant to go through the milk contract line by line before renewal, and I'd join with two other dairies to negotiate together. I'd keep about four months of costs in the bank, and not buy the new feed pusher robot I'd been thinking about. And I'd tell Elena to keep her skills sharp, especially the bits where she talks to clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a little. Not about the work, about the money around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the milk company would squeeze contracts. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Their buyers would have a machine that knows every farm's costs better than the farmer does. They'd offer each of us exactly the lowest price we'd accept. The only answer is for farmers to have the same tools and to sit down together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Sofia's salon? What would happen there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People would come less often, cuts every ten weeks instead of every six. She's been through that before, in 2009. She'd be fine, she'd just complain about it at dinner, and I'd listen.

S2.say: It's happening, so let's be practical: support people who lose jobs and retrain them, and don't let the arguing stop anyone doing anything. Both parties are making it worse by shouting.
S2.think: It doesn't touch the cows, but it might touch Elena's job and Sofia's salon if town people have less money. What worries me more is the milk company using assistants to squeeze our contract terms.
S2.do: Uses an assistant to check the milk contract line by line before renewal and joins two other dairies to negotiate together. Holds about four months of costs in the bank and puts off buying a feed pusher robot.
S2.feel: A little anxious, about the money around the work rather than the work itself.
S2.quote: Their buyers would have a machine that knows every farm's costs better than the farmer does.
S2.fieldNote: He sees an angle others miss: buyers using AI to squeeze suppliers. His answer is to use the same tools and band together with other farms. Even as an adopter he holds off on new equipment when money gets tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there has to be a deal that shares the gains, taxes on the windfall, some support for people who lose jobs, but not something that wrecks the economy. I'd vote for whoever looked like they could actually build that. I'd say farming is still a solid job, come and learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd be okay, maybe even do a bit better, because people still need milk. Land prices would go up, so the farm would be worth more on paper. But Elena probably loses her job, and the town gets poorer and angrier, and that's not a nice place to live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring Elena in properly to run the data side for us and four or five other dairies, paid by all of us, so she's got something to do. I'd keep the farm going as normal, and use the higher land value to refinance the robot loan at a better rate. And I'd keep an eye on the political side, because land taxes might come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd be doing okay while the people around me weren't, and that's uncomfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned land taxes. How would you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, mixed. I'd pay my share if it was fair, but farmers are land rich and cash poor. A tax on land value could make a dairy like mine pay out money it hasn't got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Elena think of working for her dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say yes and then argue about everything, which is what she's like. She'd probably make the farm better, too. She'd find things in my data I've been ignoring for years.

S3.say: There has to be a deal that shares the gains through windfall taxes and support for people who lose jobs, without wrecking the economy. Farming is still a solid job, so come and learn it.
S3.think: We'd be okay, maybe a bit better, because people still need milk and land would be worth more on paper. But Elena probably loses her job and the town gets poorer and angrier, which isn't a nice place to live.
S3.do: Brings Elena in to run the data side for his dairy and four or five others, paid jointly. Refinances the robot loan at a better rate using the higher land value and watches for possible land taxes.
S3.feel: Uneasy, because doing well while those around him struggle feels uncomfortable.
S3.quote: Farmers are land rich and cash poor.
S3.fieldNote: He accepts sharing gains in principle but worries a land tax would hit farms with little cash. His fix for his daughter's job loss is concrete and creative. He is comfortable, but aware of the social cost around him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, look, robots are coming to farms anyway, we've had them in dairy for years. But they can't come everywhere at once without some help for the people they replace. I'd ask for training money, not bans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, dairy might be the farm type that copes best, because we've already got robots in the shed. But my son Marco is a chef, and if robots arrive in kitchens, he's in trouble. My daughter in office work, my son in a kitchen, both of them in the firing line, and I'm the one who loves the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at the new feed and cleaning robots in the first year, probably lease rather than buy, because the price would drop fast. I'd tell Marco to look at owning a small restaurant, the people side, not just the cooking, and I'd help with some money if I could. I'd keep the herd at a hundred and eighty and not expand, because the milk price would probably fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Curious about the machines, worried for my kids. I don't like the irony of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help Marco with money. How much could you actually spare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, maybe ten thousand without touching the farm's safety money. That's a deposit on a lease for a small place, not a whole restaurant. He'd have to find the rest, and a partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marco on the phone that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I'm sorry, son, I helped build this world without thinking. Then I'd say, but people still want someone to cook for them on their birthday. A robot can make the food, but it can't remember who likes their steak rare.

S4.say: Robots are coming to farms anyway, and we've had them in dairy for years. But they can't come everywhere at once without help for the people they replace, so I'd ask for training money, not bans.
S4.think: Dairy might cope best because we already have robots in the shed. But Marco is a chef and Elena works in an office, so both my kids are in the firing line while I'm the one who loves the robots.
S4.do: Looks at leasing feed and cleaning robots rather than buying, expecting prices to drop. Holds the herd at a hundred and eighty and offers Marco about ten thousand toward leasing a small restaurant of his own.
S4.feel: Anxious, curious about the machines and worried for his children, and uncomfortable with the irony.
S4.quote: My daughter in office work, my son in a kitchen, both of them in the firing line, and I'm the one who loves the robots.
S4.fieldNote: Adam faces an uncomfortable irony: he champions robots on the farm while both his children are exposed to the same change. He reacts by leasing rather than buying and putting his limited spare cash into his son's future. His sense of guilt is quiet but real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, because of my kids, not the cows. What would help is training money for people like Marco and Elena, and a rule that farmers own their own data. And maybe some kind of loan scheme for young people to start their own businesses, the people side of things.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the hard bit of robots. Everyone thinks they make life easy, but they change your life in odd ways. The cows took to the robot in a fortnight. It took me two years to stop getting up at four to check on it.

headlineQuote: The cows took to the robot in a fortnight. It took me two years to stop getting up at four to check on it.
portrait: Adam Garcia is a 58-year-old dairy farmer with a hundred and eighty cows and two milking robots he installed in 2019, still with three years left on the loan. He uses AI every day and is the one showing others at his discussion group how, while wanting rules on who owns farm data. Through the scenarios he stays practical, banding together with other dairies to face milk buyers and finding work for his daughter in farm data. When robots come for every job, he faces the irony that both his children are exposed while he himself loves the machines.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because both his children, a chef and an office worker, would be in the firing line.
whatWouldHelp: Training money for young people like his children, rules so farmers own their data, and loans to help young people start their own businesses.
